danish.title: Tiende bog (1812) — Kapitel 3
paragraphs: Da Mikhail Ivanovitj vendte tilbage til arbejdsværelset med brevet, sad den gamle fyrste med briller på og en skygge over øjnene ved sit åbne sekretær med afskærmede stearinlys og holdt et papir i den udstrakte hånd, i en noget dramatisk positur, og læste sit manuskript — sine »Bemærkninger«, som han kaldte det — der skulle overdrages kejseren efter hans død.

Da Mikhail Ivanovitj trådte ind, stod der tårer i fyrstens øjne, fremkaldt af mindet om den tid, da det papir, han nu læste, var blevet skrevet. Han tog brevet fra Mikhail Ivanovitjs hånd, stak det i lommen, foldede sine papirer sammen og tilkaldte Alpatytj, der længe havde ventet.
Fyrsten havde en liste over ting, der skulle købes i Smolensk, og idet han gik op og ned i værelset forbi Alpatytj, der stod ved døren, gav han sine instrukser.
»For det første — brevpapir, hører du? Otte bøger, som denne prøve, med guldkant ... det skal være nøjagtigt som prøven. Fernis, laksegl, som på Mikhail Ivanovitjs liste.«
Han gik op og ned et stykke tid og kastede et blik på sine notater.
»Aflever derefter personligt et brev til guvernøren angående skødet.«
Dernæst skulle der skaffes bolte til dørene i den nye bygning, af en særlig type, fyrsten selv havde tegnet, og et læderhylster skulle bestilles til at opbevare »testamentet« i.
Instrukserne til Alpatytj tog over to timer, og stadig lod fyrsten ham ikke gå. Han satte sig, sank hen i tanker, lukkede øjnene og døsede. Alpatytj bevægede sig let.
»Nå, gå, gå! Hvis der er mere, sender jeg bud efter dig.«
Alpatytj gik ud. Fyrsten gik atter hen til sit sekretær, kiggede ind i det, fingrede ved sine papirer, lukkede det igen og satte sig ved bordet for at skrive til guvernøren.

Det var allerede sent, da han rejste sig efter at have forseglet brevet. Han ville gerne sove, men vidste, at han ikke ville kunne det, og at de mest trykkende tanker kom til ham i sengen. Så tilkaldte han Tikhon og gik rundt i værelserne med ham for at vise ham, hvor sengen skulle stilles op for natten.

Han gik rundt og kiggede i hvert hjørne. Hvert sted syntes utilfredsstillende, men det allerværste var hans sædvanlige sofa i arbejdsværelset. Den sofa var ham frygtelig, sandsynligvis på grund af de trykkende tanker, han havde haft, mens han lå dér. Det var utilfredsstillende overalt, men hjørnet bag klaveret i opholdsstuen var bedre end andre steder: dér havde han aldrig sovet endnu.
Med hjælp fra en lakaj bar Tikhon sengen ind og begyndte at stille den op.
»Nej, det er forkert! Det er forkert!« råbte fyrsten og skubbede selv sengen et par centimeter fra hjørnet og så tættere ind igen.
»Nå, endelig er jeg færdig, nu kan jeg hvile,« tænkte fyrsten og lod Tikhon klæde sig af.

Med en grimasse af ærgrelse over den anstrengelse, det krævede at rive sig fri af frakke og bukser, klædte fyrsten sig af, satte sig tungt på sengen og syntes at sidde i tanker, mens han foragteligt betragtede sine visne, gule ben. Han var ikke i tanker — han udsatte blot det øjeblik, hvor han måtte anstrenge sig for at løfte de ben op og lægge sig om. »Åh, hvor er det hårdt! Åh, gid dette slid ville høre op, og I ville lade mig gå!« tænkte han. Med sammenpressede læber foretog han den anstrengelse for tyve tusinde gang og lagde sig. Men knap havde han gjort det, før han følte sengen gynge frem og tilbage under sig, som om den åndede tungt og stødvis. Det skete for ham næsten hver nat. Han åbnede øjnene, netop som de var ved at lukke sig.

»Ingen fred, forbandede!« mumlede han, vred han vidste ikke på hvem. »Nå ja, der var noget andet, noget vigtigt, som jeg gemte til jeg kom i seng. Boltene? Nej, dem fortalte jeg ham om. Nej, det var noget — noget i dagligstuen. Fyrstinde Marja sagde noget vrøvl. Dessalles, det fjols, sagde noget. Noget i min lomme — kan ikke huske ...«
»Tikhon, hvad talte vi om ved middagen?«
»Om fyrst Mikhail ...«
»Stille, stille!« Fyrsten slog hånden i bordet. »Ja, det husker jeg nu — fyrst Andrejs brev! Fyrstinde Marja læste det op. Dessalles sagde noget om Vitebsk. Nu vil jeg læse det.«

Han fik brevet taget op af lommen og bordet — hvorpå der stod et glas limonade og et spiralformet vokslys — rykket tæt til sengen, og idet han tog brillerne på, begyndte han at læse. Først nu, i nattens stilhed, læsende det ved det svage lys under den grønne skærm, fattede han et øjeblik dets betydning.
»Franskmændene i Vitebsk — om fire dagsmarcher kan de være ved Smolensk; måske er de der allerede! Tikhon!« Tikhon sprang op. »Nej, nej, jeg behøver ingenting!« råbte han.

Han lagde brevet under lysestagen og lukkede øjnene. Og for ham rejste sig Donau i lysende middagssol: siv, den russiske lejr, og han selv som ung general uden en rynke i sit røde, sunde ansigt, kraftfuld og årvågen, der træder ind i Potjomkins broget farvede telt — og en brændende følelse af jalousi mod »favoritten« rørte sig i ham nu lige så stærkt som dengang. Han huskede alle de ord, der blev sagt ved det første møde med Potjomkin. Og han så for sig en buttet, lidt gulbleg, kort, kraftig kvinde — enkekejserinden — med sit smil og sine ord ved hendes første nådige modtagelse af ham, og derpå det samme ansigt på castrum doloris, og hans sammenstød med Zubov ved hendes kiste om retten til at kysse hendes hånd.
»Åh, hurtigere, hurtigere! At komme tilbage til den tid og få gjort det af med al denne nutid! Hurtigere, hurtigere — og lad dem lade mig i fred!«

english.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: When Michael Ivanovich returned to the study with the letter, the old prince, wearing spectacles and a shade over his eyes, was sitting at his open bureau with screened candles, holding a paper at arm's length, and reading in a somewhat dramatic pose his manuscript—his "Remarks" as he called it—which was to be sent to the Emperor after his death.

When Michael Ivanovich entered, there were tears in the prince's eyes, stirred by the memory of the time when the paper he was reading had been written. He took the letter from Michael Ivanovich, put it in his pocket, folded up his papers, and called in Alpatych, who had been waiting a long time.
The prince had a list of things to be bought in Smolensk, and walking up and down the room past Alpatych, who stood by the door, he gave his instructions.
"First, writing paper—do you hear? Eight quires, like this sample, with gilt edges... it must be exactly like the sample. Varnish, sealing wax, as on Michael Ivanovich's list."
He paced back and forth for a while and glanced at his notes.
"Then hand to the governor in person a letter about the deed."
Next, bolts for the doors of the new building were needed, and they had to be of a special design the prince had created himself, and a leather case had to be ordered to keep the "will" in.
The instructions to Alpatych took over two hours, and still the prince didn't let him go. He sat down, sank into thought, closed his eyes, and dozed off. Alpatych shifted slightly.
"Well, go, go! If anything else is needed, I'll send after you."
Alpatych went out. The prince went back to his bureau, glanced into it, fingered his papers, closed it again, and sat down at the table to write to the governor.

It was already late when he rose after sealing the letter. He wanted to sleep but knew he wouldn't be able to, and that his most depressing thoughts came to him in bed. So he called Tikhon and went through the rooms to show him where to set up the bed for that night.

He walked about examining every corner. Every place seemed unsatisfactory, but worst of all was his usual couch in the study. That couch was dreadful to him, probably because of the oppressive thoughts he'd had while lying there. It was unsatisfactory everywhere, but the corner behind the piano in the sitting room was better than the rest: he had never slept there yet.
With the help of a footman, Tikhon brought in the bedstead and began setting it up.
"That's not right! That's not right!" cried the prince, and he himself pushed it a few inches from the corner, then closer in again.
"Well, at last I've finished. Now I'll rest," the prince thought, and let Tikhon undress him.

Frowning with the effort of removing his coat and trousers, the prince undressed, sat down heavily on the bed, and seemed to be thinking as he looked disdainfully at his withered yellow legs. He wasn't really thinking, but only putting off the effort of lifting those legs and turning over on the bed. "How hard it is! Oh, if only this labor would end and You would release me!" he thought. Pressing his lips together, he made that effort for the twenty-thousandth time and lay down. But barely had he done so when the bed seemed to rock back and forth beneath him, as if it were breathing heavily and jerking. This happened nearly every night. He opened his eyes just as they were closing.

"No peace, damn them!" he muttered, angry without knowing at whom. "Ah yes, there was something else important, very important, that I was saving for when I'd be in bed. The bolts? No, I told him about those. No, it was something—something in the drawing room. Princess Mary was talking some nonsense. Dessalles, that fool, said something. Something in my pocket—can't remember..."
"Tikhon, what did we talk about at dinner?"
"About Prince Michael..."
"Quiet, quiet!" The prince slapped his hand on the table. "Yes, I know—Prince Andrew's letter! Princess Mary read it. Dessalles said something about Vitebsk. Now I'll read it."

He had the letter taken from his pocket and the table—on which stood a glass of lemonade and a spiral wax candle—moved close to the bed. Putting on his spectacles, he began reading. Only now, in the stillness of the night, reading by the faint light under the green shade, did he grasp the letter's meaning for a moment.
"The French at Vitebsk—in four days' march they could be at Smolensk; maybe they're already there! Tikhon!" Tikhon jumped up. "No, no, I don't need anything!" he shouted.

He slid the letter under the candlestick and closed his eyes. And there rose before him the Danube at bright noon: the reeds, the Russian camp, and himself a young general without a wrinkle on his ruddy face—vigorous and alert—entering Potemkin's brightly colored tent, and a burning sense of jealousy of "the favorite" stirred in him now as strongly as it had then. He recalled every word spoken at that first meeting with Potemkin. And he saw before him a plump, rather sallow, short, stout woman—the Empress Mother—with her smile and the words of her first gracious reception of him, and then that same face on the funeral bier, and the confrontation he'd had with Zubov over her coffin about his right to kiss her hand.
"Oh, let it be sooner, sooner! Let me get back to that time and be done with all this present! Sooner, sooner—and let them leave me in peace!"
